Static and single-snapshot scanners do not perform the navigation and observe where focus lands or whether anything was announced, so they report nothing.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: react-router discussion #9863 and the long-running issue #5210 ("focus not reset when route changed") document this; James Shakespeare and TestParty both prescribe moving focus to an autofocusing h1. https://github.com/remix-run/react-router/discussions/9863

allPatterns.platform: Material UI (MUI) Snackbar
allPatterns.name: Toast/snackbar not in a live region — never announced
allPatterns.description: MUI Snackbar renders transient feedback ("Item saved", "Network error") but in many real integrations it is not wired as a status/alert live region (role/aria-live missing, or the message mounts then the region's content is replaced rather than added). The toast appears and auto-dismisses purely visually; screen-reader users never learn the action's outcome. Nesting (snackbar fired from inside a dialog or menu) makes the skip even worse.
allPatterns.typicalMarkup: Item saved
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: The element only exists for a few seconds after a user action and may be gone before/at the moment of scan. Whether a polite/assertive region actually announced depends on AT behavior and on the timing/insertion method, which a DOM linter cannot evaluate. axe will not flag a plain div with text as a 4.1.3 failure.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: MUI issue #29080 "Snackbars not read by screen reader" and #30097 (snackbar from a button inside a dialog not read); maintainers/community note toasts are often not implemented as live regions. https://github.com/mui/material-ui/issues/29080

allPatterns.platform: Font Awesome (web-font / CSS pseudo-element icons)
allPatterns.name: Decorative icon-font glyph read aloud (or interactive icon with no name)
allPatterns.description: Font Awesome's web-font method renders a glyph via a CSS ::before pseudo-element on an empty <i>/<span>. If the author omits aria-hidden="true", some AT/browsers expose the private-use Unicode glyph as garbage or a literal character name. Conversely, when the icon IS the only content of a link/button and is hidden (or carries no text alternative), the control has no accessible name at all.
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: Whether the glyph is decorative (needs aria-hidden) or meaningful (needs a label) is a semantic call. An empty <i> with classes has no text for a linter to evaluate, and the icon-only-link-with-no-name case is sometimes caught by axe but not when a stray whitespace/title gives a spurious name; deciding the name is wrong/missing in context needs human review.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: Font Awesome's own accessibility docs state web-font icons must be manually given aria-hidden if decorative and role=img + visually-hidden text if meaningful. https://docs.fontawesome.com/web/dig-deeper/accessibility

allPatterns.platform: Inline SVG icon system (Heroicons, Lucide, Feather, Material Symbols inlined)
allPatterns.name: Icon-only button/link with no accessible name (SVG provides none)
allPatterns.description: A button or link whose only content is an inline <svg> with no <title>, no aria-label on the control, and no visually-hidden text. Screen readers announce just "button" / "link". Even when a <title> is added inside the SVG, several browser+SR combinations fail to surface it as the control's name, so it must be on the button.
allPatterns.typicalMarkup:
<button class="icon-btn">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="M..."/></svg>
</button>
<!-- announced as just "button" -->
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe and Lighthouse DO reliably flag a button/link with an empty accessible name ("Buttons must have discernible text"), so a linter catches the no-name case. (Choosing a CORRECT label, however, would need human judgment — but the bare detection is automatable, hence flagged false.)
allPatterns.realWorldNote: Sara Soueidan and CSS-Tricks document that there is no reliable way to use an SVG as the sole accessible name and that icon-only controls need aria-label on the control. https://www.sarasoueidan.com/blog/accessible-icon-buttons/

allPatterns.platform: Custom div/span "button" (React component with role="button")
allPatterns.name: Label-in-name mismatch: aria-label differs from visible text
allPatterns.description: A component renders a clickable element showing one visible label but sets an aria-label/aria-labelledby that says something different (e.g. visible "Submit", aria-label "Submit form"; or visible "Buy" with aria-label "Add to cart"). Speech-input users who say the visible word cannot activate it, and the announced name conflicts with what is seen.
allPatterns.typicalMarkup: Submit
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe's label-content-name-mismatch rule catches some cases, but it only fires when the visible text is NOT contained in the accessible name; many real mismatches (paraphrases, icon+text where the visible text is partly present, or labelledby pointing at a different node) slip through, and judging whether the names are semantically equivalent for a user requires reading both as a human.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: Deque axe rule label-content-name-mismatch and W3C ARIA14 / SC 2.5.3 Label in Name describe this; Ben Myers warns against aria-label on elements with visible text. https://dequeuniversity.com/rules/axe/4.7/label-content-name-mismatch

allPatterns.platform: Tailwind CSS / Tailwind UI utility classes
allPatterns.name: focus:outline-none with no replacement focus ring
allPatterns.description: Developers apply Tailwind's focus:outline-none (often to kill the default blue ring on inputs/buttons) but never add a focus-visible:ring/outline replacement. Keyboard users get no visible focus indicator as they tab through forms and menus, making the UI unusable without a mouse.
allPatterns.typicalMarkup:
<button class="focus:outline-none px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 text-white">
  Save
</button>
<!-- on Tab focus, nothing visible changes -->
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe/Lighthouse do not evaluate whether a visible focus indicator appears on :focus — there is no reliable automated check for 2.4.7. Detecting the missing ring requires actually tabbing and visually observing each control's focus state, i.e. human or pixel-diff judgment, especially since outline-none renders a transparent (not removed) outline.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: Tailwind's own docs warn that outline-none must be paired with an accessible focus state and recommend focus-visible: utilities; community guidance repeatedly flags focus:outline-none misuse. https://tailwindcss.com/docs/outline-style

allPatterns.platform: CMS-driven card/teaser components (React/Vue rendered from CMS data)
allPatterns.name: Repeated generic "Read more" / "Learn more" links
allPatterns.description: A reusable Card component renders a fixed call-to-action link ("Read more", "Learn more", "Details") for every item, with the descriptive title rendered as separate text outside the link. A screen-reader user pulling up the links list hears "Read more, Read more, Read more..." with no way to tell the destinations apart; in-context the link text alone is non-descriptive.
allPatterns.typicalMarkup:
Annual Report 2025

Summary text...

Read more
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: The link has non-empty text, so "discernible text" checks pass. Some tools heuristically warn on the literal string "read more," but they cannot judge whether the surrounding context (the heading) is programmatically associated, whether the destinations actually differ, or whether the text is adequately descriptive — that is a semantic, contextual reading.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: Vision Australia and WCAG SC 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) describe non-descriptive "Read more" links as a classic failure; common in CMS card components. https://www.visionaustralia.org/business-consulting/digital-access/blog/how-to-make-read-more-links-accessible

allPatterns.platform: Bootstrap default theme (buttons, alerts, form-validation, placeholders)
allPatterns.name: Default palette variants fail contrast (btn-warning, btn-info, alerts, placeholder)
allPatterns.description: Bootstrap's stock color variants — notably .btn-warning, .btn-info, .btn-success (dark text or white text on light fills) and muted placeholder text — produce text and UI-component contrast below 4.5:1 / 3:1 against light backgrounds. Sites that adopt the defaults unmodified inherit the failures across every page.
allPatterns.typicalMarkup:
<button class="btn btn-warning">Continue</button>
<!-- #ffc107 fill with near-black text region edges; white-text variants ~2-3:1 -->
<input class="form-control" placeholder="Search...">
<!-- placeholder ~ #6c757d on white -->
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: This one IS reliably automatable — axe/Lighthouse compute text contrast ratios and flag failing button/placeholder colors. Flagged false because a contrast checker catches it; the only caveat is large-text thresholds and overlay images, which can need human review.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: Bootstrap's own accessibility page admits default palette combinations may fall below WCAG contrast; twbs/bootstrap issue #25126 tracks failing AA combinations. https://github.com/twbs/bootstrap/issues/25126

allPatterns.platform: E-commerce product page (React/Vue store, Shopify/SFCC swatch components)
allPatterns.name: Color-only variant swatches with no text label or non-color selected state
allPatterns.description: Product color/variant options render as colored squares (often div with a background-color and a click handler) with no accompanying text name, and the selected swatch is indicated only by a colored ring. Users who cannot perceive color cannot tell which variant they are choosing or which is currently selected; the swatches may also lack accessible names entirely.
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: Whether information (the color name / which is selected) is conveyed by color ALONE requires understanding what the UI means and checking for an equivalent non-color cue (text, checkmark, label). Tools cannot determine that a background-color is the sole carrier of meaning, nor that the selected-ring is color-only.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: Section508 and WCAG 1.4.1 cover color-only selection; Craftshift and the EAA-2025 swatch guidance note most Shopify swatch apps render unlabeled clickable divs. https://craftshift.com/shopify-european-accessibility-act-swatches/

allPatterns.platform: Ant Design Form / Form.Item
allPatterns.name: Validation error not programmatically associated with the field
allPatterns.description: Ant Design's Form renders inline validation errors visually beneath the input, but historically did not set aria-invalid on the control nor aria-describedby pointing at the error text, and labels were not always tied to inputs. The error appears in red text but is not announced when the field is focused, and the field is not exposed as invalid.
allPatterns.typicalMarkup: Please enter a valid email
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: The error text exists in the DOM, so it is visible to a scanner, but verifying that it is PROGRAMMATICALLY tied to the right input (and announced on focus / on submit) requires triggering validation and inspecting the runtime aria relationships; the visual-only error with a missing association is not reliably flagged by static rules.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: Ant Design issues #36730 (set aria-invalid/aria-describedby on invalid inputs), #28748 (link error messages to field), and #16268 ("Forms in Ant Design are not accessible"). https://github.com/ant-design/ant-design/issues/36730

allPatterns.platform: Bootstrap Modal (and hand-rolled React modals)
allPatterns.name: Background page not inert / aria-hidden focus conflict behind modal
allPatterns.description: When a Bootstrap/custom modal opens, the underlying page is not made inert and is not hidden from AT (or, conversely, aria-hidden="true" is placed on an ancestor that still contains the focused trigger). Screen-reader users can read and tab into the page behind the dialog, and focus can land on aria-hidden content, producing the "focusable element inside aria-hidden" conflict.
allPatterns.typicalMarkup: ...
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe flags aria-hidden containing a focusable element only when the snapshot is in that exact state; whether the background is truly inert / focus is trapped is a runtime, interaction-driven property. Confirming a SR can reach behind-modal content or that Tab escapes requires actually operating the dialog with the keyboard/AT.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: Bootstrap issue #29769 and MDN's aria-modal docs cover the inert/aria-hidden tradeoff; the focusable-inside-aria-hidden conflict is a frequent audit finding. https://github.com/twbs/bootstrap/issues/29769

allPatterns.platform: MUI Autocomplete / Select (combobox)
allPatterns.name: Stale aria-activedescendant / aria-controls on closed combobox
allPatterns.description: MUI's Autocomplete leaves aria-controls pointing at a listbox id before the listbox exists, and keeps aria-activedescendant on the input set to the last-highlighted option id after the popup closes. Screen readers can announce a phantom "active" option that is no longer on screen, or reference a control that is not in the DOM, confusing combobox navigation.
allPatterns.typicalMarkup:
<input role="combobox"
  aria-expanded="false"
  aria-controls="listbox-1"        <!-- listbox not in DOM -->
  aria-activedescendant="option-7"> <!-- popup is closed -->
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: The attributes are syntactically valid (valid id references when the listbox is open), so static ARIA-attribute validity checks pass. The defect is a state/timing inconsistency between the visual popup state and the aria-* values, which only manifests during interaction and must be judged against expected combobox behavior.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: MUI issue #18133 "Some WAI-ARIA attributes are incorrect" documents aria-controls set before the listbox exists and aria-activedescendant not cleared on close. https://github.com/mui/material-ui/issues/18133

allPatterns.platform: jQuery UI / Bootstrap Tabs & Accordion
allPatterns.name: div/anchor "tab" widgets lacking tab roles and arrow-key support
allPatterns.description: Older jQuery UI and many Bootstrap-derived tab/accordion implementations render tabs as <a>/<li> or plain divs that toggle panels via click, without role="tablist"/"tab"/"tabpanel", without aria-selected/aria-controls, and without the expected arrow-key roving-tabindex behavior. Screen readers do not recognize the tab pattern and keyboard users cannot move between tabs with arrow keys.
allPatterns.typicalMarkup:
• Details
  • Reviews
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: Plain anchors with hrefs are individually valid and focusable, so structural linters see nothing wrong. Recognizing that this SHOULD be the ARIA tabs pattern (and that arrow-key navigation and aria-selected are absent) requires understanding the intended widget semantics and testing keyboard interaction.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: WAI-ARIA APG tabs pattern requires roles + arrow-key support; legacy jQuery UI / Bootstrap tab markup commonly ships without them, a recurring audit finding for interactive widgets.

allPatterns.platform: React conditionally-rendered form error summary / aria-live status
allPatterns.name: Submit-time errors rendered but not announced; focus not moved
allPatterns.description: On form submit, a React app conditionally renders an error summary or per-field messages into the DOM, but the container is not a live region and focus is not moved to it. Sighted users see red errors; screen-reader users get no announcement and remain focused on the submit button, unaware the submission failed.
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: The error text is present in the post-submit DOM, so a snapshot scan sees content, not a failure. Whether it was ANNOUNCED (live region) or focus was moved to it is a dynamic, interaction-and-timing property invisible to static/single-snapshot tools.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: TetraLogical and Up Your A11y describe accessible error-summary patterns requiring focus management or a live region; conditionally-rendered React errors routinely omit both. https://tetralogical.com/blog/2024/10/21/foundations-form-validation-and-error-messages/

allPatterns.platform: React/Vue placeholder-as-label inputs (Tailwind/MUI styled)
allPatterns.name: Placeholder used as the only label
allPatterns.description: Inputs styled by component libraries frequently use the placeholder attribute as the sole label (no <label>, no aria-label). The hint disappears once the user types, low-contrast placeholder text fails contrast, and there is no programmatic label — screen readers may announce nothing or only "edit text".
allPatterns.typicalMarkup:
<input type="email" placeholder="Email address">
<!-- no <label for>, no aria-label; placeholder is the only cue -->
allPatterns.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe reliably flags inputs with no accessible name ("Form elements must have labels"), so the bare missing-label case is automatable — flagged false. The residual judgment (is a placeholder an ADEQUATE instruction even when a label exists, contrast of the placeholder) can still need a human, but detection of no-label is a linter check.
allPatterns.realWorldNote: WCAG 3.3.2 and broad guidance treat placeholder-as-label as a failure (text vanishes on input, low contrast); extremely common in utility-CSS/component-styled forms.

1.1.1.platform: Wix ProGallery / Wix Pro Gallery & Slideshow image blocks
1.1.1.name: Filename-as-alt-text on auto-imported gallery images
1.1.1.description: When a user drags images into a Wix gallery/slideshow without filling the optional alt field, the rendered gets either an empty/absent alt or the raw upload filename echoed into a title/alt-like attribute, so informative product/portfolio images announce as 'IMG_4821' or 'DSC0093-2-1024x768' or nothing at all. The alt field is optional in the editor and routinely skipped.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: An alt attribute IS present and non-empty, so axe/Lighthouse 'image-alt' passes. Only a human reading the page can tell that 'IMG_4821~mv2.jpg' is a meaningless filename rather than a description of what the image conveys, and whether the image is informative (needs real alt) or decorative (needs alt="").
1.1.1.realWorldNote: WebAIM 2025 Million found 55.5% of pages have alt-text problems; Wix support docs make the gallery alt field optional, and Wix accessibility guides repeatedly flag ProGallery/Slideshow images as the most common missing/inadequate-alt source. https://support.wix.com/en/article/accessibility-preparing-your-images-and-galleries

1.1.1.name: Triple-redundant 'Read More →' links sharing one destination
1.1.1.description: Each summary item auto-emits the thumbnail image, the post title, AND a 'Read More →' link, all three pointing to the same post URL. Screen-reader users tabbing the link list hear 'Read More, link / Read More, link / Read More, link' with no way to distinguish posts, and the same destination is reachable three times. The 'Read More →' text cannot be edited or removed through built-in settings.
1.1.1.typicalMarkup: Spring Tips Read More →
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Each <a> has non-empty text ('Read More →'), so link-name checks pass; the redundancy/ambiguity is only a problem when the links are read out of context as a list, which requires human judgment about whether the link purpose is determinable. Tools can't know the three links go to the same place is intended vs. confusing.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Amy Carney's hands-on Squarespace audit: 'Redundant links: image, heading, and Read More all link to same destination' and the Read More link cannot be customized or unlinked. https://theamycarney.com/2024/04/02/observations-on-squarespace-accessibility/

1.1.1.platform: WordPress Media Library / auto-alt plugins (Auto Image Alt Text from Filename, Image Attributes Pro) on any Twenty* or builder theme
1.1.1.name: Alt text is the raw filename (or template default 'image')
1.1.1.description: WordPress core never auto-populates the alt attribute, so editors either leave it blank or install a plugin that copies the filename into alt. The img then carries semantically useless alt like 'IMG_4521', 'DSC00231-1024x683', 'hero-banner-final-v2' or a slug like 'untitled-1'. It passes the 'has alt' check but conveys nothing; informative images get garbage and decorative images get noise.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse only check that alt is present and non-empty; a filename string satisfies that. Deciding whether alt actually describes the image's purpose, or whether the image is decorative and should have empty alt, requires looking at the image and the surrounding context.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: WordPress core does not set alt from anything; WPBeginner and the 'Auto Image Attributes From Filename' plugin (200k+ installs) explicitly populate alt from the filename. https://wordpress.org/plugins/auto-image-attributes-from-filename-with-bulk-updater/ and https://brutalbusiness.com/automatically-set-the-wordpress-image-title-alt-text-other-meta/

1.1.1.platform: Elementor Icon Box / Icon List widget (Font Awesome icon fonts)
1.1.1.name: Icon-only link/button whose accessible name is the icon glyph or empty
1.1.1.description: Icon Box and social-icon widgets render a link wrapping only a Font Awesome <i> with no text. The accessible name comes out empty (empty link) or, when the icon font exposes a glyph/private-use character, a screen reader announces a meaningless symbol name. CSS pseudo-element icons (::before content) can be read aloud as random characters bearing no relation to the visible icon.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: When the accessible name is truly empty, axe catches it (link has no discernible text). But when the icon font leaks a glyph name or a pseudo-element character into the name, the link is technically 'named' and tools pass it while the announced name ('private-use-F07A') is meaningless — judging that requires hearing what's announced vs. seeing the cart icon.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Elementor docs and abrightclearweb note Icon widgets 'create empty links and adjacent identical links'; Divi review notes CSS pseudo-element icons cause screen readers to 'announce the symbol's name, which has no semantic relationship.' https://www.abrightclearweb.com/elementor-accessibility/ and https://elevagedigital.com/improving-wordpress-divi-accessibility/

1.1.1.platform: Elementor Image Carousel / Slides widget, Divi Slider, Smart Slider 3
1.1.1.name: Auto-advancing carousel: icon-only controls + slide content/links hidden from AT
1.1.1.description: Slider widgets auto-rotate with no clearly labeled pause/stop control. Prev/next arrows are icon-only with empty accessible names; pagination dots are unlabeled buttons. Off-screen slides are not consistently hidden from the accessibility tree, so screen-reader users encounter duplicate/moving content and links to slides they can't see.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Empty arrow/dot names are partially catchable, but judging that hidden slides leak focusable links into the tab order, and that there is no labeled pause control, requires observing the running carousel and its focus behavior across slide states.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Elementor audit: 'Images in the carousel advance automatically every three seconds with no mechanism for pausing, stopping, or hiding.' https://www.accessibilitychecker.org/blog/elementor-website-accessibility/

1.1.1.platform: WordPress theme demo import / starter templates (Astra, OceanWP, Elementor Kits, Divi Layouts)
1.1.1.name: Placeholder demo content left in production — default title, lorem ipsum, stock alt
1.1.1.description: One-click demo imports populate the site with template defaults that editors forget to replace: the page <title> stays 'My WordPress Site' / 'Just another WordPress site' tagline, headings and links read 'Lorem ipsum dolor', CTA buttons say 'Button Text', and stock images carry the kit's generic alt. Titles don't uniquely describe the page; link text is meaningless Latin.
1.1.1.typicalMarkup:
Lorem Ipsum Dolor

Click Here
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: A <title> of 'Just another WordPress site' is present and non-empty (2.4.2 passes a presence check); lorem-ipsum link text is non-empty. Recognizing the content is unreplaced placeholder that fails to describe topic/purpose is a semantic judgment a linter can't make.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Demo/starter imports use lorem ipsum and template defaults; WPBeginner documents importing dummy content; 'Just another WordPress site' is the stock tagline. https://www.wpbeginner.com/wp-themes/how-to-add-dummy-content-for-theme-development-in-wordpress/

1.1.1.platform: WooCommerce / Elementor product loop on Storefront, Astra, Divi shops
1.1.1.name: Color/variant swatches conveyed by color only; 'Add to cart' names not unique
1.1.1.description: Product variation swatches are colored squares/links with no text or accessible name ('Red', 'Blue' is visual-only), so the choice is unperceivable without color. In the shop grid every product's 'Add to cart' / 'Select options' button has the same name, indistinguishable by product when navigating by button.
1.1.1.typicalMarkup: Add to cart
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Color-only meaning (1.4.1) is not statically detectable — a tool can't know the red square MEANS 'red' with no text backup. Repeated 'Add to cart' names are valid names. Both require understanding what the visual conveys and the by-button navigation experience.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: WooCommerce color-swatch plugins render color-only links; equalizedigital and WebAIM repeatedly flag color-only controls and duplicate 'add to cart' button names as a top WordPress-shop barrier. https://equalizedigital.com/accessibility-checker/

1.1.1.platform: Shopify Dawn theme — product variant picker (color)
1.1.1.name: Color-only variant swatches with no text alternative
1.1.1.description: Color variant options render as colored circles/squares (radio inputs visually replaced by background-color chips). The only way to know which color is which is to see the chip; the accessible name is often the hex/handle or absent, so a screen reader announces 'option 1, option 2' or just the color value, and there is no non-color cue distinguishing selected vs available swatches. Color is the sole means of conveying the choice.
1.1.1.typicalMarkup: Color
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: The radio inputs are technically labeled (the <label for> exists and the value attribute carries the color name), so axe/Lighthouse see a valid, named form control and pass it. They cannot perceive that the swatch communicates the choice purely through a CSS background-color, nor judge whether the visible chip and the accessible name actually correspond, nor whether selection state has a non-color indicator.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Shopify Dawn ships swatches as color chips and merchants add color-only swatches via tutorials (made4uo.com swatch guide; Dawn issue #3112 on color swatches). Audits of Dawn flag color contrast and ARIA on swatches. https://github.com/Shopify/dawn/issues/3112 ; https://testparty.ai/blog/shopify-dawn-theme-accessibility

1.1.1.name: Alt text is the filename or a generic default
1.1.1.description: Product images imported via CSV/feed or drag-drop bulk upload inherit alt text equal to the filename (e.g. 'IMG_4823' or 'product-1_2048x.jpg') or a templated default like 'Product image' / the store name. The image is informational (shows the actual product) but the alt conveys nothing about color, style, or what is shown.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: An alt attribute is present and non-empty, which is exactly what axe/WAVE check for — so it passes 'images have alt text'. Recognizing that 'DSC_0234_2048x' or 'Product image' is meaningless and fails to describe the actual product requires reading the alt against the visible image: a semantic/visual human judgment of quality, not presence.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Baymard found 55% of ecommerce sites don't communicate informational image content via alt; WCAG.com and Siteimprove note auto/bulk imports default to filenames; AI alt-text apps exist precisely because the default is filename/blank. https://baymard.com/blog/informational-image-accessibility

1.1.1.platform: Magento Luma / third-party review widgets — star ratings
1.1.1.name: Star rating rendered with CSS width %, no text alternative
1.1.1.description: Average rating shows as filled/empty stars implemented as a background-image bar with inline width (e.g. width:80%). There is no aria-label or visually-hidden text, so screen readers announce nothing, or announce a raw '80%' with no unit, instead of 'Rated 4 out of 5 stars'. Same in third-party Shopify review apps.
1.1.1.typicalMarkup: Rating:
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: There is no to require alt on — the stars are CSS background images, which automated scanners ignore entirely. A title='80%' may exist but tools won't judge that '80%' is meaningless as a rating. Determining that this visual is conveying a 4-of-5 rating that needs a textual equivalent is a human contextual/visual judgment.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Magento Luma uses CSS-width rating bars; TestParty's Shopify barriers list cites third-party 'review widgets with star ratings without text alternatives'. https://testparty.ai/blog/beyond-alt-text-hidden-shopify-accessibility-barriers

1.1.1.platform: Webflow CMS dynamic image / multi-image field
1.1.1.name: CMS-bound images ship with empty or filename alt at scale
1.1.1.description: Static images can get alt text in the Designer, but CMS Collection images default to empty alt unless the author explicitly binds an alt field, and multi-image (gallery) fields ALWAYS render alt="". Editors rarely populate a dedicated alt field, so dozens of meaningful content images (product photos, team headshots, article heroes) publish with empty or auto-filename alt across every collection-list and template page.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: alt="" is VALID markup (correct for decorative images), so a linter cannot know a CMS hero photo is meaningful content that needs a description rather than a deliberately-decorative image. When alt is the filename, axe/WAVE treat it as 'has alt' and pass it — judging that 'product-7f3a91' or 'team_photo_final_v2' is useless requires a human to compare the text to the actual image.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Finsweet/SAYU SEO guides document that Webflow CMS and multi-image fields default to empty alt and require manual field binding, and Webflow's own audit panel only inspects static images, not dynamic CMS images: https://finsweet.com/seo/article/cms-image-dynamic-alt-tags and https://help.webflow.com/hc/en-us/articles/33961330170643-Include-alt-text-on-images

1.1.1.platform: Framer / Webflow link styled by color only (nav, inline text links, variant swatches)
1.1.1.name: Information conveyed by color alone (links, swatches, states)
1.1.1.description: Designers distinguish links from body text, active nav items, or product color/variant swatches using color only — no underline, no text label, no shape/border difference. Color swatches in particular carry the variant name ('Red', 'Forest') purely as a colored circle with no text or accessible name.
1.1.1.typicalMarkup: Read our terms first.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Tools can't tell that the only cue distinguishing a link from surrounding text is color (they'd have to compare the link's styling to adjacent text and the rest of the page). For color swatches, an unlabeled colored button looks like a generic empty button; recognizing it ENCODES a named option that's conveyed by color alone needs human/visual judgment.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Use-of-color is a top WCAG failure category; design-tool defaults frequently strip link underlines and rely on hue. Background on the swatch/color-only pattern and 1.4.1: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/use-of-color.html and contrast/use-of-color prevalence: https://www.studiolimb.com/guides/wcag-color-contrast-guide.html

1.1.1.platform: Webflow / Framer hero text baked into an exported image or background
1.1.1.name: Images of text in hero/banner graphics
1.1.1.description: To preserve exact typography, designers export a hero headline, promotional banner, or pricing graphic as a flattened PNG/JPG (or set it as a CSS background-image) instead of live text. The 'text' is pixels: it can't be resized/restyled, and if alt is missing or generic the content is also lost to screen readers.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Nothing in the markup declares that an image's pixels contain readable text; an automated tool can't OCR/decide an image is 'an image of text' that could have been real text (1.4.5) vs. a legitimate photo/logo. Even an image with alt passes 1.1.1 — judging it's text-as-image needs human visual inspection.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Design-to-site workflows commonly flatten styled headlines to images to preserve fonts; 1.4.5 prohibits images of text except logos/essential cases: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/images-of-text.html

1.1.1.name: Decorative icon-font glyph read aloud (or interactive icon with no name)
1.1.1.description: Font Awesome's web-font method renders a glyph via a CSS ::before pseudo-element on an empty <i>/<span>. If the author omits aria-hidden="true", some AT/browsers expose the private-use Unicode glyph as garbage or a literal character name. Conversely, when the icon IS the only content of a link/button and is hidden (or carries no text alternative), the control has no accessible name at all.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Whether the glyph is decorative (needs aria-hidden) or meaningful (needs a label) is a semantic call. An empty <i> with classes has no text for a linter to evaluate, and the icon-only-link-with-no-name case is sometimes caught by axe but not when a stray whitespace/title gives a spurious name; deciding the name is wrong/missing in context needs human review.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Font Awesome's own accessibility docs state web-font icons must be manually given aria-hidden if decorative and role=img + visually-hidden text if meaningful. https://docs.fontawesome.com/web/dig-deeper/accessibility

1.1.1.platform: Inline SVG icon system (Heroicons, Lucide, Feather, Material Symbols inlined)
1.1.1.name: Icon-only button/link with no accessible name (SVG provides none)
1.1.1.description: A button or link whose only content is an inline <svg> with no <title>, no aria-label on the control, and no visually-hidden text. Screen readers announce just "button" / "link". Even when a <title> is added inside the SVG, several browser+SR combinations fail to surface it as the control's name, so it must be on the button.
1.1.1.typicalMarkup:
<button class="icon-btn">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="M..."/></svg>
</button>
<!-- announced as just "button" -->
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe and Lighthouse DO reliably flag a button/link with an empty accessible name ("Buttons must have discernible text"), so a linter catches the no-name case. (Choosing a CORRECT label, however, would need human judgment — but the bare detection is automatable, hence flagged false.)
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Sara Soueidan and CSS-Tricks document that there is no reliable way to use an SVG as the sole accessible name and that icon-only controls need aria-label on the control. https://www.sarasoueidan.com/blog/accessible-icon-buttons/

1.1.1.platform: E-commerce product page (React/Vue store, Shopify/SFCC swatch components)
1.1.1.name: Color-only variant swatches with no text label or non-color selected state
1.1.1.description: Product color/variant options render as colored squares (often div with a background-color and a click handler) with no accompanying text name, and the selected swatch is indicated only by a colored ring. Users who cannot perceive color cannot tell which variant they are choosing or which is currently selected; the swatches may also lack accessible names entirely.
1.1.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Whether information (the color name / which is selected) is conveyed by color ALONE requires understanding what the UI means and checking for an equivalent non-color cue (text, checkmark, label). Tools cannot determine that a background-color is the sole carrier of meaning, nor that the selected-ring is color-only.
1.1.1.realWorldNote: Section508 and WCAG 1.4.1 cover color-only selection; Craftshift and the EAA-2025 swatch guidance note most Shopify swatch apps render unlabeled clickable divs. https://craftshift.com/shopify-european-accessibility-act-swatches/

1.3.1.name: Multiple H1s — one per article title on a listing page
1.3.1.description: Squarespace blog index and collection pages output the site/page title as an H1 and then render EACH article title in the feed as its own H1, producing many H1s on one page. Screen-reader users navigating by heading level get a flat, ambiguous outline with no single page topic and no h2-level grouping of the list.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup:
Journal

First Post

Second Post
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Multiple H1s are technically valid HTML5 and most automated rules only warn (or not at all) about it; whether the heading hierarchy actually communicates the page's structure is a semantic judgment. axe flags 'page-has-heading-one' as satisfied, not violated.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Amy Carney's Squarespace audit: 'Multiple H1 headings on single page (one per article title) despite page already having H1.' https://theamycarney.com/2024/04/02/observations-on-squarespace-accessibility/

1.3.1.name: System page reuses generic title and has no H1
1.3.1.description: The default 404 page (and some system pages) ships with no option for an H1 and inherits a non-unique page title, so AT users who land there get a page with no main heading and a <title> that doesn't say it's a 'Page Not Found' page, leaving them disoriented about where they are.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup:
<title>My Studio</title>
<main><!-- 404 copy but no <h1> --></main>
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: A <title> is present and non-empty, so 'document-title' passes; whether it actually describes THIS page (vs. being the generic site title repeated) is a semantic comparison a human must make. A missing h1 is at most a warning, not a hard failure, in most scanners.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Amy Carney's Squarespace audit: 404 page has 'no H1 heading option available' and is 'missing a unique page title.' https://theamycarney.com/2024/04/02/observations-on-squarespace-accessibility/

1.3.1.name: Visual lists of items not exposed as semantic lists
1.3.1.description: Galleries, summary grids, and icon rows render as a pile of sibling divs/anchors rather than <ul><li>, so screen-reader users never hear 'list, 12 items' and lose the count and grouping that sighted users get from the visual grid.
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Divs are valid markup and there's no rule that says 'these siblings should be a list' — recognizing that a visual grid conveys a list relationship that the markup fails to express is a semantic/visual judgment automated tools cannot make.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Amy Carney's Squarespace audit: 'Image galleries not auto-generated as semantic lists.' https://theamycarney.com/2024/04/02/observations-on-squarespace-accessibility/

1.3.1.platform: Squarespace / Wix contact & booking forms (custom-styled fields)
1.3.1.name: Placeholder used as the only label; errors not programmatically tied to fields
1.3.1.description: Custom-styled form fields rely on the placeholder as the visible label (no <label>), so the field's name vanishes once the user types, and error messages are shown as text near the form rather than associated with the offending input (no aria-describedby, no aria-invalid, no focus to the error).
1.3.1.typicalMarkup: Please enter a valid email.
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe can catch an input with NO accessible name, but a placeholder often supplies a name so the input 'passes'; that the label disappears on input and that the visible error isn't programmatically linked to its field are judgment/behavioral checks. Whether helper text constitutes adequate instructions is semantic.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Wix accessibility guides warn that Wix Forms/Bookings with custom field styling can leave 'labels and error messages not programmatically associated'; Amy Carney found Squarespace form errors not linked to inputs or focused. https://accessibe.com/blog/knowledgebase/wix-website-accessibility

1.3.1.platform: Divi Contact Form module / Elementor Form widget with placeholder-only fields
1.3.1.name: Form field labeled only by placeholder (or label visually hidden by default)
1.3.1.description: Divi's Contact Form hides labels by default and relies on placeholder text; Elementor forms are frequently configured the same way. The input has no <label>/aria-label, only a placeholder, so once the user types the label vanishes and screen readers may announce the field as unlabeled. Required-field asterisks are color-only with no text alternative.
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: This one is largely linter-catchable: axe flags inputs with no programmatic label. It is included for completeness, though confirming the placeholder text is the only labeling and that the asterisk's meaning is color-only still benefits from human review.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Divi review: 'The Divi Contact Form module hides labels by default, making it difficult for screen readers to interpret form inputs.' https://reciteme.com/us/news/divi-accessibility/

1.3.1.platform: Elementor Accordion / Toggle widget, Divi Toggle/Accordion module
1.3.1.name: Custom accordion header not keyboard-operable / wrong tabindex / missing aria-expanded
1.3.1.description: Accordion headers are <div>/<a href="#"> with a jQuery click handler. The clickable element either isn't focusable, or has the wrong tabindex (Elementor puts tabindex on the wrong child so the control is invisible to keyboard), and Enter/Space don't toggle because the handler only listens for click. aria-expanded is missing or, in some builder versions, slapped onto a <summary> where it is invalid.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup:
Section One
...
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: role=tab with no working keyboard handler can look structurally fine to a scanner; some tools flag missing aria-expanded but not the click-only handler. Confirming Enter/Space actually toggle the panel, and that focus lands and the expanded state is announced, requires keyboard testing.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Elementor issue #23335 'Accordion and Toggle have broken accessibility'; #11246 'aria-expanded not used'; community: 'JQuery click event handler cannot be triggered via keypress.' https://github.com/elementor/elementor/issues/23335 and https://testpros.com/accessibility/making-elementor-essential-addons-accordion-accessible/

1.3.1.platform: Gutenberg blocks / page-builder sections used as visual styling (Heading block, Divi Text module set to H-tag)
1.3.1.name: Heading levels chosen for font size — skipped levels and visual-only headings
1.3.1.description:
Editors pick heading tags by how big they look. A section header is set to H4 because H2 'looks too big', producing H1 then H4 with no H2/H3. Conversely, bold styled text that visually functions as a heading is left as a

, so the document outline has no entry. Builders make every text element's tag a free-form dropdown, so structure tracks visual size, not meaning.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup:
Welcome

Our Services

Pricing
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss:
Tools can flag a skipped level (H1->H4) but cannot decide that styled bold

SHOULD be a heading, nor whether a heading is descriptive of the section it labels. That mapping of visual prominence and meaning to correct level/semantics is human judgment.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Learn WordPress and WP handbook warn against using headings for visual styling / skipping levels. https://learn.wordpress.org/tutorial/using-headings-for-accessibility-and-seo/ ; Gutenberg document outline only warns, doesn't enforce.

1.3.1.platform: Elementor Tabs widget / Beaver Builder Tabs / Divi Tabs module
1.3.1.name: Tab panel content not associated/announced; div tabs missing roles
1.3.1.description: Builder 'tabs' render as styled divs. Either the tablist/tab/tabpanel roles and aria-controls/aria-selected are absent (so it's just clickable divs), or the roles exist but the panel content isn't reliably exposed when a tab is activated. Selecting a tab by keyboard may not move focus or announce the newly revealed panel.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup:
• Description
  • Reviews
...
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Plain divs with click handlers raise no role/value error in a scanner (nothing claims to be a tab). Where roles do exist, confirming the active panel's content is actually announced on switch needs screen-reader testing, not static analysis.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Beaver Builder review: with tabs 'the content of an expanded tab isn't reliably read out.' https://wpshout.com/beaver-builder-accessibility/

1.3.1.platform: Twenty* core themes & most premium/builder themes — landmark structure
1.3.1.name: Ambiguous duplicate nav landmarks and structure built from role-less divs
1.3.1.description: Builder sections wrap everything in generic <div>s with no landmark roles, so the page has no programmatic structure beyond the theme header/footer. Where multiple <nav> regions exist (primary menu, footer menu, breadcrumbs) they share no distinguishing aria-label, so a screen-reader user hears 'navigation, navigation, navigation' with no way to tell them apart.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup:
...primary menu...
...footer menu...
...
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Duplicate unlabeled nav landmarks may or may not be flagged depending on the tool, and missing landmark structure built from divs isn't an error per se. Judging that two 'navigation' regions are ambiguous and that the page lacks a sensible landmark map needs human review of how it's announced.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Builder pages are notorious for div-soup with no landmarks; Divi historically shipped no skip link and weak landmark labeling. https://www.accessgo.de/en/divi-accessibility-overview-requirements-solutions-and-practical-examples/

1.3.1.platform: Shopify / generic theme — sale price markup on product card and PDP
1.3.1.name: Sale price reads as two bare numbers with no Was/Now context
1.3.1.description: On-sale prices show the original price with a CSS strikethrough next to the discounted price. The strikethrough is purely visual; screen readers announce something like '$50.00 $30.00' with no indication which is the regular price and which is the sale price, and no 'Was/Now' or 'Sale' context. Visually-hidden context spans are missing.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup: $50.00 $30.00
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Both prices are present as real text, so there is no missing-alt or empty-element violation to flag. The <s> element conveys 'no longer accurate' semantically to almost no screen reader by default, but tools don't treat its absence of announcement as an error. Deciding that the output '$50 $30' is confusing and needs 'Was/Now' wording requires understanding the sale semantics — a human contextual judgment.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Well documented by AccessiCart ('Accessible sale prices') and the Shopify partners blog 'Developing Shopify Themes with Accessibility in Mind'; fix is visually-hidden 'Was'/'Now' spans. https://accessicart.com/accessible-sale-prices/ ; https://a11y.tips/blog/discounted-price/

1.3.1.platform: WooCommerce — store notices on page load (waitlist / coupon / stock)
1.3.1.name: Page-load notice not programmatically a status message
1.3.1.description: WooCommerce renders informational notices (e.g. 'To join the waitlist, click Notify me', coupon applied, 'only 2 left') as a styled div shown when the page renders. The notice has no role=status/alert and focus is not placed on it, so on a fresh page load it is visible but never announced to screen reader users.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup: To join the waitlist, please click the "Notify me" button.
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: There is no markup defect: contrast is fine and the text exists in the DOM. Whether a given message is a 'status message' that must be announced (vs. ordinary body copy) is a semantic judgment about its purpose and timing; axe/Lighthouse cannot infer intent and do not flag missing role=status on plain divs.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Filed directly against WooCommerce core as a WCAG 4.1.3 failure: 'message is visually displayed, but screen readers do not announce it because it has not been programmatically defined as a status message, and focus is not set on the message when the page loads.' https://github.com/woocommerce/woocommerce/issues/59383

1.3.1.platform: Shopify / WooCommerce — AJAX filter / faceted search sidebar
1.3.1.name: Facet filtering updates grid silently; no result-count announcement
1.3.1.description: Selecting a filter checkbox (size, color, price) re-renders the product grid via AJAX with no page reload. The new result count ('24 products') and any 'No results' state are not in a live region, so screen reader users don't know the grid changed or how many products remain. Some themes also replace native checkboxes with styled divs that lose keyboard operability.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup: 24 products
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: On the initial static snapshot the markup is valid (labeled checkboxes, a count div). The defect appears only when a filter fires and content swaps without an announcement — a runtime behavior. Whether the count and no-results state qualify as status messages requiring aria-live is an intent-based judgment scanners can't make.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Equalize Digital's FacetWP audit and Scott O'Hara's 'dynamic results' guidance cover exactly this; accessibility-test.org documents ecommerce faceted-search live-region gaps. https://equalizedigital.com/testing-facetwp-for-accessibility/ ; https://accessibility-test.org/blog/compliance/accessibility-for-e-commerce-product-filtering-and-faceted-search/

1.3.1.name: Lightbox opens without focus trap, dialog role, or labeled close
1.3.1.description: Webflow's built-in Lightbox opens an overlay but does not trap focus (Tab leaves the modal to the page behind it), has no role=dialog / aria-modal, no accessible name on the dialog, and the close 'X' is an unlabeled icon. Esc behavior and focus return to the trigger are not handled.
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: A missing focus trap is a behavioral property: nothing in the static markup is 'invalid', so axe/Lighthouse cannot detect that Tab escapes the open overlay. The unlabeled close MIGHT be flagged, but confirming the dialog lacks a name and that focus returns to the trigger requires opening it and operating it by keyboard.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Documented that the Webflow lightbox lacks a focus trap (users can tab out), is missing a descriptive accessible name on the dialog, and needs custom code/ARIA to fix: https://www.gracefulwebstudio.com/blog-articles/webflow-video-lightbox-accessibility-and-focus-management and Webflow's own checklist task 'Ensure modals are keyboard navigable': https://webflow.com/accessibility/checklist/task/ensure-modals-are-keyboard-navigable

1.3.1.name: Heading hierarchy from visual size: skipped levels and multiple H1s
1.3.1.description: Designers style text layers by visual size and Framer lets each text layer be tagged H1–H6 (or left as a paragraph/div). The result is non-sequential heading levels (H1 → H4), several H1s on one page, decorative big text marked as a heading, or real section headings left as plain styled divs.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup:
Acme

Build faster

Features

Pricing
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Skipped levels and multiple H1s are partly linter-detectable, but the high-value errors are semantic: deciding that a big styled <div> SHOULD be a heading, or that an <h4> is functioning as the section title, requires understanding the page's meaning and visual structure — automated checks can't infer intended document outline.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: AudioEye's Framer review stresses that simply tagging headings isn't enough and that missing/out-of-order/non-descriptive headings break navigation; Framer's per-layer heading control makes mis-tagging easy: https://www.audioeye.com/post/framer-offers-accessibility-features-but-are-they/

1.3.1.name: Form inputs labeled only by placeholder; aria-label mismatches visible text
1.3.1.description: Bubble inputs commonly ship with a placeholder instead of a programmatic label, or developers paste an aria-label that differs from the visible text. On submit, native required/format errors are not associated with the field (no aria-describedby), so error identification and suggestion are absent for screen-reader users.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup: Invalid
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: If an aria-label is present, axe sees 'input has an accessible name' and passes — it can't know the placeholder disappeared on input or that the aria-label ('Work email') contradicts the visible 'Email address' (a Label-in-Name mismatch). Confirming the error div isn't programmatically tied to the field and isn't announced requires interaction.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Bubble accessibility guidance flags placeholder-as-label and warns that replacing visible labels with aria-label causes a screen-reader/visible-text mismatch; Bubble's own marketplace app audited ~60% accessible: https://www.rapidevelopers.com/bubble-tutorial/designing-accessibility-mind-bubble and https://forum.bubble.io/t/is-bubble-accessible-does-it-comply-with-ada-and-wcag/287361

1.3.1.name: Generic page <title> and weak heading semantics on exported Notion sites
1.3.1.description: Notion-published pages frequently inherit a generic or duplicated <title> (workspace/page name patterns), and content blocks rely heavily on styled divs; toggles, callouts, and 'columns' don't expose the semantic relationships sighted users perceive. Multiple pages can share an indistinct title, and toggle disclosure widgets often lack proper expanded/collapsed state.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup:
▸ Details
...
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: A <title> exists, so 2.4.2 passes automatically; judging that it's non-descriptive/duplicated across pages needs human comparison. Missing aria-expanded on a toggle MIGHT be linted, but deciding that a styled callout/column block carries structural meaning that isn't conveyed programmatically is a semantic judgment.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Notion accessibility assessments document alt-text, contrast, and tabbing/focus problems and difficulty operating interactive elements with assistive tech: https://ixd.prattsi.org/2024/12/assessing-the-accessibility-of-notion/ and https://www.templates4notion.com/newsletters/better-notion-accessibility

1.3.1.name: Validation error not programmatically associated with the field
1.3.1.description: Ant Design's Form renders inline validation errors visually beneath the input, but historically did not set aria-invalid on the control nor aria-describedby pointing at the error text, and labels were not always tied to inputs. The error appears in red text but is not announced when the field is focused, and the field is not exposed as invalid.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup: Please enter a valid email
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: The error text exists in the DOM, so it is visible to a scanner, but verifying that it is PROGRAMMATICALLY tied to the right input (and announced on focus / on submit) requires triggering validation and inspecting the runtime aria relationships; the visual-only error with a missing association is not reliably flagged by static rules.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: Ant Design issues #36730 (set aria-invalid/aria-describedby on invalid inputs), #28748 (link error messages to field), and #16268 ("Forms in Ant Design are not accessible"). https://github.com/ant-design/ant-design/issues/36730

1.3.1.name: Stale aria-activedescendant / aria-controls on closed combobox
1.3.1.description: MUI's Autocomplete leaves aria-controls pointing at a listbox id before the listbox exists, and keeps aria-activedescendant on the input set to the last-highlighted option id after the popup closes. Screen readers can announce a phantom "active" option that is no longer on screen, or reference a control that is not in the DOM, confusing combobox navigation.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup:
<input role="combobox"
  aria-expanded="false"
  aria-controls="listbox-1"        <!-- listbox not in DOM -->
  aria-activedescendant="option-7"> <!-- popup is closed -->
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: The attributes are syntactically valid (valid id references when the listbox is open), so static ARIA-attribute validity checks pass. The defect is a state/timing inconsistency between the visual popup state and the aria-* values, which only manifests during interaction and must be judged against expected combobox behavior.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: MUI issue #18133 "Some WAI-ARIA attributes are incorrect" documents aria-controls set before the listbox exists and aria-activedescendant not cleared on close. https://github.com/mui/material-ui/issues/18133

1.3.1.name: div/anchor "tab" widgets lacking tab roles and arrow-key support
1.3.1.description: Older jQuery UI and many Bootstrap-derived tab/accordion implementations render tabs as <a>/<li> or plain divs that toggle panels via click, without role="tablist"/"tab"/"tabpanel", without aria-selected/aria-controls, and without the expected arrow-key roving-tabindex behavior. Screen readers do not recognize the tab pattern and keyboard users cannot move between tabs with arrow keys.
1.3.1.typicalMarkup:
• Details
  • Reviews
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Plain anchors with hrefs are individually valid and focusable, so structural linters see nothing wrong. Recognizing that this SHOULD be the ARIA tabs pattern (and that arrow-key navigation and aria-selected are absent) requires understanding the intended widget semantics and testing keyboard interaction.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: WAI-ARIA APG tabs pattern requires roles + arrow-key support; legacy jQuery UI / Bootstrap tab markup commonly ships without them, a recurring audit finding for interactive widgets.

1.3.1.name: Placeholder used as the only label
1.3.1.description: Inputs styled by component libraries frequently use the placeholder attribute as the sole label (no <label>, no aria-label). The hint disappears once the user types, low-contrast placeholder text fails contrast, and there is no programmatic label — screen readers may announce nothing or only "edit text".
1.3.1.typicalMarkup:
<input type="email" placeholder="Email address">
<!-- no <label for>, no aria-label; placeholder is the only cue -->
1.3.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe reliably flags inputs with no accessible name ("Form elements must have labels"), so the bare missing-label case is automatable — flagged false. The residual judgment (is a placeholder an ADEQUATE instruction even when a label exists, contrast of the placeholder) can still need a human, but detection of no-label is a linter check.
1.3.1.realWorldNote: WCAG 3.3.2 and broad guidance treat placeholder-as-label as a failure (text vanishes on input, low contrast); extremely common in utility-CSS/component-styled forms.

1.3.2.name: DOM/reading order diverges from visual order on overlapping layouts
1.3.2.description: Wix's drag-anywhere canvas positions elements absolutely; the algorithm that derives DOM order from on-screen coordinates can mis-order overlapping, stacked, or strip-based sections, so keyboard Tab order and screen-reader reading order jump around (e.g., footer CTA before main content, a caption before its image, a price before the product name).
1.3.2.typicalMarkup:
Add to cart
Handmade Mug — $24
1.3.2.whyAutoToolsMiss: Automated tools generally cannot determine the 'correct' meaningful sequence — they don't know the visually-intended reading order, so they can't tell that DOM order contradicts it. Detecting the mismatch requires a human comparing the visual layout to the tab/reading order.
1.3.2.realWorldNote: Wix Engineering describes building an algorithm to make DOM order reflect visual position precisely because the canvas otherwise breaks navigation order; Wix support has a dedicated 'Checking and Adjusting a Site's DOM Order' article. https://www.wix.engineering/post/the-story-of-making-wix-accessible

1.3.2.platform: Webflow / Framer absolute-positioned layout (CSS grid-area, position:absolute, flex order)
1.3.2.name: Visual order diverges from DOM/tab order in free-canvas layouts
1.3.2.description: On a free design canvas, authors drag elements into a visual arrangement while the DOM source order stays whatever was authored. Absolute positioning, CSS order, and grid placement make the reading/tab order jump around — e.g., a CTA visually at top-left is last in the DOM, or a sidebar reads before the main column for a screen reader.
1.3.2.typicalMarkup:
Primary CTA
Legal footnote
Headline
1.3.2.whyAutoToolsMiss: Both the DOM order and the CSS are individually valid; determining that the resulting tab/reading order is 'illogical' relative to the visual layout requires a human to compare what they SEE to the order focus actually moves — automated tools have no model of the intended visual narrative.
1.3.2.realWorldNote: Webflow's checklist 'Ensure focus order is logical' explicitly warns that arranging elements with CSS instead of the Navigator yields nonlinear/illogical focus order; WCAG technique C27 covers DOM-vs-visual order: https://webflow.com/accessibility/checklist/task/ensure-focus-order-is-logical and https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG20-TECHS/C27.html

1.4.1.platform: Elementor Form widget / Divi Contact Form / WPForms — submission feedback
1.4.1.name: Success/error toast not in a live region; errors flagged by color only
1.4.1.description: After AJAX form submit, the success or error message is injected into a <div> that is not a live region and not focused, so screen readers never announce it. Inline validation marks invalid fields with a red border/red text only, with no programmatic error association and no text describing what's wrong or how to fix it.
1.4.1.typicalMarkup: Your message was sent!
1.4.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: The success div is valid HTML; nothing in the static DOM signals it should announce on change. Detecting that a dynamically-inserted status isn't announced requires triggering the submit and observing AT silence. Color-only error indication also needs visual judgment that no text/icon backs the red.
1.4.1.realWorldNote: ARIA live-region guidance: 'create an empty element and then update its content' — builder messages don't. https://a11y-blog.dev/en/articles/aria-live-regions/ ; matches harness 4.1.3 / 3.3.x shadow lanes.

1.4.1.platform: WooCommerce / Elementor product loop on Storefront, Astra, Divi shops
1.4.1.name: Color/variant swatches conveyed by color only; 'Add to cart' names not unique
1.4.1.description: Product variation swatches are colored squares/links with no text or accessible name ('Red', 'Blue' is visual-only), so the choice is unperceivable without color. In the shop grid every product's 'Add to cart' / 'Select options' button has the same name, indistinguishable by product when navigating by button.
1.4.1.typicalMarkup: Add to cart
1.4.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Color-only meaning (1.4.1) is not statically detectable — a tool can't know the red square MEANS 'red' with no text backup. Repeated 'Add to cart' names are valid names. Both require understanding what the visual conveys and the by-button navigation experience.
1.4.1.realWorldNote: WooCommerce color-swatch plugins render color-only links; equalizedigital and WebAIM repeatedly flag color-only controls and duplicate 'add to cart' button names as a top WordPress-shop barrier. https://equalizedigital.com/accessibility-checker/

1.4.1.platform: Shopify Dawn theme — product variant picker (color)
1.4.1.name: Color-only variant swatches with no text alternative
1.4.1.description: Color variant options render as colored circles/squares (radio inputs visually replaced by background-color chips). The only way to know which color is which is to see the chip; the accessible name is often the hex/handle or absent, so a screen reader announces 'option 1, option 2' or just the color value, and there is no non-color cue distinguishing selected vs available swatches. Color is the sole means of conveying the choice.
1.4.1.typicalMarkup: Color
1.4.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: The radio inputs are technically labeled (the <label for> exists and the value attribute carries the color name), so axe/Lighthouse see a valid, named form control and pass it. They cannot perceive that the swatch communicates the choice purely through a CSS background-color, nor judge whether the visible chip and the accessible name actually correspond, nor whether selection state has a non-color indicator.
1.4.1.realWorldNote: Shopify Dawn ships swatches as color chips and merchants add color-only swatches via tutorials (made4uo.com swatch guide; Dawn issue #3112 on color swatches). Audits of Dawn flag color contrast and ARIA on swatches. https://github.com/Shopify/dawn/issues/3112 ; https://testparty.ai/blog/shopify-dawn-theme-accessibility

1.4.1.platform: Shopify / generic theme — sale price markup on product card and PDP
1.4.1.name: Sale price reads as two bare numbers with no Was/Now context
1.4.1.description: On-sale prices show the original price with a CSS strikethrough next to the discounted price. The strikethrough is purely visual; screen readers announce something like '$50.00 $30.00' with no indication which is the regular price and which is the sale price, and no 'Was/Now' or 'Sale' context. Visually-hidden context spans are missing.
1.4.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Both prices are present as real text, so there is no missing-alt or empty-element violation to flag. The <s> element conveys 'no longer accurate' semantically to almost no screen reader by default, but tools don't treat its absence of announcement as an error. Deciding that the output '$50 $30' is confusing and needs 'Was/Now' wording requires understanding the sale semantics — a human contextual judgment.
1.4.1.realWorldNote: Well documented by AccessiCart ('Accessible sale prices') and the Shopify partners blog 'Developing Shopify Themes with Accessibility in Mind'; fix is visually-hidden 'Was'/'Now' spans. https://accessicart.com/accessible-sale-prices/ ; https://a11y.tips/blog/discounted-price/

1.4.1.platform: Magento Luma / third-party review widgets — star ratings
1.4.1.name: Star rating rendered with CSS width %, no text alternative
1.4.1.description: Average rating shows as filled/empty stars implemented as a background-image bar with inline width (e.g. width:80%). There is no aria-label or visually-hidden text, so screen readers announce nothing, or announce a raw '80%' with no unit, instead of 'Rated 4 out of 5 stars'. Same in third-party Shopify review apps.
1.4.1.typicalMarkup: Rating:
1.4.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: There is no to require alt on — the stars are CSS background images, which automated scanners ignore entirely. A title='80%' may exist but tools won't judge that '80%' is meaningless as a rating. Determining that this visual is conveying a 4-of-5 rating that needs a textual equivalent is a human contextual/visual judgment.
1.4.1.realWorldNote: Magento Luma uses CSS-width rating bars; TestParty's Shopify barriers list cites third-party 'review widgets with star ratings without text alternatives'. https://testparty.ai/blog/beyond-alt-text-hidden-shopify-accessibility-barriers

1.4.1.name: Field errors shown as red text only, not associated with the input
1.4.1.description: On checkout submit, invalid fields turn red and a message like 'This field is required' appears, but the message is a sibling div not linked via aria-describedby/aria-errormessage, the input has no aria-invalid, and color is the only cue marking which fields failed. Screen reader users tabbing the form don't hear which fields are in error or why.
1.4.1.typicalMarkup: This field is required.
1.4.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: The error text exists and the label is associated, so structural scanners pass. They cannot verify at runtime that submitting produced an error that is (a) tied to the right field programmatically and (b) not communicated by red color alone. Confirming the association and that the message is meaningful requires submitting the form and inspecting the error/field relationship — a human/runtime judgment.
1.4.1.realWorldNote: Generic but rampant in ecommerce checkout; DigitalA11y and AccessiCart describe exactly this 3.3.1 pattern (red-only, unassociated errors) and call it out for checkout flows. https://accessicart.com/wcag-level-a-sc-3-3-1-error-identification/ ; https://www.digitala11y.com/understanding-sc-3-3-1-error-identification/

1.4.1.platform: Generic ecommerce — required-field marking on cart/checkout/newsletter forms
1.4.1.name: Required fields indicated by red asterisk/color only
1.4.1.description: Checkout, account, and newsletter signup forms mark required inputs with a red asterisk styled purely via color (no 'required' word, no required/aria-required attribute, asterisk not in the label text). Users who don't perceive the color, or screen reader users, don't learn the field is mandatory until submission fails.
1.4.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: The label is associated and present, so the form passes label checks. Whether 'required' is conveyed by more than color, whether the asterisk's meaning is explained, and whether aria-required is set are partly structural but partly contextual — tools don't flag a red asterisk as a use-of-color failure because they can't tie the color to the 'required' meaning. Recognizing the instruction is missing needs human review.
1.4.1.realWorldNote: TestParty 'Beyond Alt Text' lists 'red asterisks only marking required fields without text labels' as a Shopify use-of-color (1.4.1) barrier. https://testparty.ai/blog/beyond-alt-text-hidden-shopify-accessibility-barriers

1.4.1.platform: Framer / Webflow link styled by color only (nav, inline text links, variant swatches)
1.4.1.name: Information conveyed by color alone (links, swatches, states)
1.4.1.description: Designers distinguish links from body text, active nav items, or product color/variant swatches using color only — no underline, no text label, no shape/border difference. Color swatches in particular carry the variant name ('Red', 'Forest') purely as a colored circle with no text or accessible name.
1.4.1.typicalMarkup: Read our terms first.
1.4.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Tools can't tell that the only cue distinguishing a link from surrounding text is color (they'd have to compare the link's styling to adjacent text and the rest of the page). For color swatches, an unlabeled colored button looks like a generic empty button; recognizing it ENCODES a named option that's conveyed by color alone needs human/visual judgment.
1.4.1.realWorldNote: Use-of-color is a top WCAG failure category; design-tool defaults frequently strip link underlines and rely on hue. Background on the swatch/color-only pattern and 1.4.1: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/use-of-color.html and contrast/use-of-color prevalence: https://www.studiolimb.com/guides/wcag-color-contrast-guide.html

1.4.1.platform: E-commerce product page (React/Vue store, Shopify/SFCC swatch components)
1.4.1.name: Color-only variant swatches with no text label or non-color selected state
1.4.1.description: Product color/variant options render as colored squares (often div with a background-color and a click handler) with no accompanying text name, and the selected swatch is indicated only by a colored ring. Users who cannot perceive color cannot tell which variant they are choosing or which is currently selected; the swatches may also lack accessible names entirely.
1.4.1.whyAutoToolsMiss: Whether information (the color name / which is selected) is conveyed by color ALONE requires understanding what the UI means and checking for an equivalent non-color cue (text, checkmark, label). Tools cannot determine that a background-color is the sole carrier of meaning, nor that the selected-ring is color-only.
1.4.1.realWorldNote: Section508 and WCAG 1.4.1 cover color-only selection; Craftshift and the EAA-2025 swatch guidance note most Shopify swatch apps render unlabeled clickable divs. https://craftshift.com/shopify-european-accessibility-act-swatches/

1.4.3.platform: Carrd single-page sites (default sections / overlay text)
1.4.3.name: Low-opacity white text fails contrast while looking 'designed'
1.4.3.description: Carrd templates frequently set body/caption text in semi-transparent white (rgba(255,255,255,0.3) or 0.15) over photographic or gradient backgrounds. It reads as a tasteful muted style to the designer but falls far below 4.5:1, and over a varying photo background the effective ratio changes per region.
1.4.3.typicalMarkup: Subscribe for updates
1.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: Automated contrast tools can't reliably compute the ratio of text over a CSS background-image/photo (no solid color to sample) and often skip or guess; the rgba opacity composited against an image is exactly the case scanners punt on, leaving a human to sample the rendered pixels.
1.4.3.realWorldNote: Audit of a Carrd site found 50 automated issues incl. text using rgba(255,255,255,0.3) and rgba(255,255,255,0.15) weakening contrast. https://dev.to/yuridevat/accessibility-check-2-195p

1.4.3.name: Light-gray body/caption text below 4.5:1 in the default palette
1.4.3.description: Many Wix templates ship with light-gray secondary text (captions, subtitles, footer text, form helper text) that fails AA contrast out of the box. Because it's the template default, it propagates everywhere the user adds that text style without them realizing it's non-compliant.
1.4.3.typicalMarkup: Crafted with care since 2014
1.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: This one IS reliably caught by axe/Lighthouse when text sits on a solid color — included for completeness. The judgment-light cases (solid background, real text node) are auto-detectable; only the over-image variants need a human.
1.4.3.realWorldNote: Wix ADA guides repeatedly cite 'many Wix templates use light gray text that fails contrast requirements' as a default-template problem. https://accessibe.com/blog/knowledgebase/wix-website-accessibility

1.4.3.platform: Squarespace image-caption overlay (dark-overlay style) & gallery captions
1.4.3.name: Caption text over a dark-overlay/photo overlay fails contrast
1.4.3.description: The built-in 'dark overlay' caption style puts light caption text over a semi-transparent dark scrim on top of a photo. On bright or busy images the scrim isn't enough and the foreground/background ratio drops below 4.5:1 in some regions of the image while passing in others.
1.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: Text over a translucent scrim over a photo has no single computable background color; scanners cannot evaluate per-pixel contrast across the image and typically skip it, so a human must visually sample worst-case regions.
1.4.3.realWorldNote: Amy Carney's Squarespace audit: 'Dark overlay option produces poor foreground/background color contrast' for image captions. https://theamycarney.com/2024/04/02/observations-on-squarespace-accessibility/

1.4.3.platform: Shopify Dawn / Debut — sale badges and disabled/sold-out states
1.4.3.name: Insufficient contrast on sale badges and disabled buttons
1.4.3.description: 'Sale' / 'Sold out' badges and disabled 'Add to cart' buttons use light or theme-accent colors (e.g. light pink on white, grey-on-grey) that fall below 4.5:1 for the text, and the badge's non-text boundary can fall below 3:1. Common in default and lightly-customized Dawn/Debut palettes.

1.4.3.platform: Bootstrap default theme (buttons, alerts, form-validation, placeholders)
1.4.3.name: Default palette variants fail contrast (btn-warning, btn-info, alerts, placeholder)
1.4.3.description: Bootstrap's stock color variants — notably .btn-warning, .btn-info, .btn-success (dark text or white text on light fills) and muted placeholder text — produce text and UI-component contrast below 4.5:1 / 3:1 against light backgrounds. Sites that adopt the defaults unmodified inherit the failures across every page.

<button class="btn btn-warning">Continue</button>
<!-- #ffc107 fill with near-black text region edges; white-text variants ~2-3:1 -->
<input class="form-control" placeholder="Search...">
<!-- placeholder ~ #6c757d on white -->

1.4.3.name: Placeholder used as the only label
1.4.3.description: Inputs styled by component libraries frequently use the placeholder attribute as the sole label (no <label>, no aria-label). The hint disappears once the user types, low-contrast placeholder text fails contrast, and there is no programmatic label — screen readers may announce nothing or only "edit text".
1.4.3.typicalMarkup:
<input type="email" placeholder="Email address">
<!-- no <label for>, no aria-label; placeholder is the only cue -->
1.4.3.whyAutoToolsMiss: axe reliably flags inputs with no accessible name ("Form elements must have labels"), so the bare missing-label case is automatable — flagged false. The residual judgment (is a placeholder an ADEQUATE instruction even when a label exists, contrast of the placeholder) can still need a human, but detection of no-label is a linter check.
1.4.3.realWorldNote: WCAG 3.3.2 and broad guidance treat placeholder-as-label as a failure (text vanishes on input, low contrast); extremely common in utility-CSS/component-styled forms.

1.4.5.platform: Webflow / Framer hero text baked into an exported image or background
1.4.5.name: Images of text in hero/banner graphics
1.4.5.description: To preserve exact typography, designers export a hero headline, promotional banner, or pricing graphic as a flattened PNG/JPG (or set it as a CSS background-image) instead of live text. The 'text' is pixels: it can't be resized/restyled, and if alt is missing or generic the content is also lost to screen readers.
1.4.5.whyAutoToolsMiss: Nothing in the markup declares that an image's pixels contain readable text; an automated tool can't OCR/decide an image is 'an image of text' that could have been real text (1.4.5) vs. a legitimate photo/logo. Even an image with alt passes 1.1.1 — judging it's text-as-image needs human visual inspection.
1.4.5.realWorldNote: Design-to-site workflows commonly flatten styled headlines to images to preserve fonts; 1.4.5 prohibits images of text except logos/essential cases: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/images-of-text.html

1.4.10.platform: Divi / Elementor on mobile — fixed-width builder sections and reflow
1.4.10.name: Fixed-pixel-width sections break reflow at 320px / 400% zoom
1.4.10.description: Builder sections built with fixed pixel widths / absolute positioning / large negative margins cause horizontal scrolling or content loss at 320 CSS px (or 400% zoom). 2.1.1.name: Div with onClick acting as a button — wrong/absent role, no keyboard, name mismatch

2.1.1.platform: Shopify / BigCommerce — quick-view modal (Add to cart from grid)
2.1.1.name: Quick-view modal keyboard trap / no focus return
2.1.1.description: Quick-view modals open over the product grid. Two common failures: (a) focus stays on the underlying page so keyboard users tab through background content behind the overlay, or (b) focus enters the modal but Escape doesn't close it and Tab can cycle but never escape, and on close focus is not returned to the triggering 'Quick view' button — keyboard users are stranded or lose their place.

The trap, the missing Escape handler, and the failure to restore focus to the trigger are dynamic, interaction-time behaviors that require actually tabbing through the open modal and closing it — automated DOM snapshots don't exercise focus flow or key handlers.
